hints: Focus on the two separate halide clues here, the steamy fumes made with concentrated sulfuric acid and the colour plus ammonia behaviour of the silver precipitate.
Steamy white fumes that give a white precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia point specifically to $\text{HCl}$ gas and $\text{AgCl}$, so Q must contain chloride ions.
Now check which chloride in the list is a white solid that dissolves easily in water to release those chloride ions for testing.
walkthrough:
**Decode the fumes test**

Think of concentrated sulfuric acid as a proton donor that displaces volatile hydrogen halides from solid halide salts. White steamy fumes mean hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, was formed.

$$\text{Cl}^{-}(s) + \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}(l) \rightarrow \text{HCl}(g) + \text{HSO}_{4}^{-}$$

**Decode the silver nitrate test**

The $\text{HCl}$ gas dissolves and gives $\text{Cl}^{-}(aq)$, which forms a precipitate with $\text{Ag}^{+}(aq)$. A white precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia is the classic result for $\text{AgCl}$.

$$\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{Cl}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s, \text{white})$$

**Combine clues and check solubility**

Both tests tell us Q contains chloride ions, $\text{Cl}^{-}$. Q is also described as a white crystalline solid which dissolves easily in water, so it must be a soluble chloride salt.

$$\text{Q(s)} \xrightarrow{\text{water}} \text{cation}(aq) + \text{Cl}^{-}(aq)$$

**Pick the matching compound**

Sodium chloride, $\text{NaCl}$, fits perfectly. It is white, very soluble, and supplies $\text{Cl}^{-}$ for both reactions. The other options are insoluble or contain bromide.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{AgCl}$ is white and contains chloride, but it is famously insoluble in water and would not dissolve easily. Q must dissolve to give a solution, so this fails the first sentence.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{NaBr}$ is white and soluble, but bromide gives a different result. With concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ it gives $\text{HBr}$ which is oxidised to brown bromine fumes, and with $\text{AgNO}_{3}$ it gives a cream precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$ which is only soluble in concentrated ammonia, not dilute.
options.C: Correct. $\text{NaCl}$ is a white crystalline solid, very soluble in water. With concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ it gives steamy white $\text{HCl}$ fumes, which form white $\text{AgCl}$ with $\text{AgNO}_{3}$. $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_{3}$ to form the complex $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_{3})_{2}]^{+}$.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{PbBr}_{2}$ contains bromide, not chloride, so it would not give white $\text{HCl}$ fumes or white $\text{AgCl}$. It is also only sparingly soluble in cold water, not easily soluble, and would give a cream $\text{AgBr}$ precipitate.
